title: Rijksmuseum or Van Gogh Museum: which to choose with half a day, and how the timed tickets work
subtitle: Two museums on the same lawn in Amsterdam, both entered by time slot. What each holds, how long it takes, and how to do both.
excerpt: The Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum stand a few minutes apart on Museumplein in Amsterdam. What each one is, how long each takes, which to choose with half a day, how the timed tickets work, and what the partner sells for both.
secondary_keywords: Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum in one day
longtail_phrases: should I visit the Rijksmuseum or the Van Gogh Museum
can you do the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum in one day
how long does the Van Gogh Museum take
do you need to book the Rijksmuseum in advance
is The Starry Night in the Van Gogh Museum
meta_title: Rijksmuseum or Van Gogh Museum: which one to choose
meta_description: Two Amsterdam museums on one lawn, both on timed tickets. What each holds, how long it takes, which to pick with half a day, and how to do both.

featured_image.alt: The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam seen across the lawn of Museumplein, with people sitting on the grass

content_html:
[place attraction="museumplein" city="amsterdam"]

Vincent van Gogh died in July 1890, having sold almost nothing. His paintings, several hundred of them, passed to his brother Theo, an art dealer in Paris, who died six months later. They then belonged to Theo's widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, who was twenty-eight and had a baby son.

She took them home to the Netherlands. Over the next thirty years she lent them to exhibitions, sold a few with care, and edited the letters Vincent had written to Theo, which were published in 1914. Her son kept the collection together and in 1962 passed it to a foundation, and the museum built for it opened in 1973. That is why the largest collection of Van Gogh in the world stands a few minutes on foot from the national museum of the Netherlands, and why visitors with half a day in Amsterdam ask the same question: which one?

Two museums on one lawn

Museumplein is a long lawn south of the canal ring. The Rijksmuseum closes its northern end: a building of 1885 by Pierre Cuypers, with a public passage through the middle that cyclists use all day. The Van Gogh Museum is on the western side, in a plain block of 1973 and a rounded wing added in 1999. Beside it are the Stedelijk Museum, for modern art and design, and the small private Moco Museum.

Both of the large museums admit visitors by start time, booked in advance. In spring and summer neither should be left to the day itself.

What the Rijksmuseum is

It is the museum of the whole country: eight centuries of Dutch art and history, some eight thousand objects in eighty rooms. The heart of it is on the upper floor. The Gallery of Honour is a long hall of side chapels holding Vermeer's Milkmaid and Little Street, Rembrandt's Jewish Bride, Frans Hals and Jan Steen, and it leads to the Night Watch of 1642, which has a hall of its own. For some years that painting has been examined and restored where it hangs, inside a glass enclosure, so you may see it through glass.

Vermeer's Milkmaid, painted about 1660, in the Gallery of Honour. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Around this are Delft blue pottery, dolls' houses made for rich merchants' wives, ship models, an Asian pavilion and the old library. Two hours are enough for the famous rooms if you go straight upstairs. Three to four is a comfortable visit.

The library of the Rijksmuseum, which visitors look into from a balcony. Photo: Sebastian Koppehel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

What the Van Gogh Museum is

It is one life, told in order, floor by floor. The dark Dutch years end with the Potato Eaters of 1885. In Paris the colours brighten, and he paints himself again and again because he cannot pay models. Then come Arles, with the Sunflowers, the Bedroom and the Yellow House; the asylum at Saint-Rémy, where he painted Almond Blossom for the birth of his nephew, the baby of the story above; and the last weeks at Auvers, with Wheatfield with Crows.

Almond Blossom, painted in 1890 for the birth of the nephew who later founded the museum. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

The collection has about two hundred of his paintings and five hundred drawings, of which a part is on show. Two things people expect are not here: The Starry Night is in New York, and Café Terrace at Night is in the Kröller-Müller Museum, in the east of the country. A visit takes an hour and a half to two hours. The rooms are small for the numbers, and the middle of the day is crowded.

The rounded wing of the Van Gogh Museum, added in 1999, seen from the lawn. Photo: Sebastian Koppehel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Which one, with half a day

  • Choose the Rijksmuseum if you want breadth: Rembrandt, Vermeer, the building itself, and the story of a small country that was briefly the richest in Europe. It asks for more time and a plan.
  • Choose the Van Gogh Museum if you would sooner follow one story from start to finish. It is shorter, easier to do well, and less tiring.
  • If one of them is sold out, it is usually the Van Gogh Museum, which is much smaller. The Rijksmuseum is the easier one to get into at short notice.
  • Both in one day is possible. Book the two slots at least three hours apart, take the Rijksmuseum first while you are fresh, and eat in between.

How the timed tickets work

  • The time is an entry time. Arrive within the window printed on the ticket. Once inside you can stay until closing.
  • Book online. The Van Gogh Museum has for years sold its tickets online only, and the Rijksmuseum asks every visitor to reserve a start time. Do not count on a desk at the door.
  • Under eighteen is free at both, and young visitors still need a ticket with a time on it.
  • The quiet hours are the first slot of the morning and the last two hours of the afternoon.

Opening hours are on our pages for the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Rijksmuseum ticket with a highlights audio tour and a city walk includes entry at a time you choose, commentary on the main works in the partner's app, and an audio walk afterwards towards the eastern side of the old centre.
  • The Rijksmuseum highlights audio tour on its own has no ticket. You book entry yourself.
  • The Van Gogh Museum ticket is entry at a time slot and nothing else. A second listing adds an audio tour in the app, with directions from room to room, and a third is that audio tour without the ticket.
  • The Moco Museum ticket with a city audio tour is entry to Moco and an audio walk through Amsterdam. The partner's commentary does not cover the inside of the museum.

Other listings carry Van Gogh's name and are different places elsewhere in the city, such as an immersive light show. If it is the paintings you want, the title has to say Van Gogh Museum. For the audio tours, bring earphones.

These are the Museumplein tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="museum amsterdam" match="rijksmuseum,gogh,moco" limit="4"]

What is free on Museumplein

The lawn, the passage under the Rijksmuseum, where musicians play for the echo, and the museum's formal gardens, with their sculptures and fountain, cost nothing. So does its great glass-roofed entrance hall, as far as the ticket barriers.

From Central Station, trams reach Museumplein in about a quarter of an hour. On foot it is half an hour, straight through the canal ring.

From here

The Stedelijk Museum is next door to the Van Gogh Museum, and the Concertgebouw faces the far end of the lawn. The Vondelpark is five minutes to the west. Ten minutes to the east is De Pijp, with the street market of Albert Cuypstraat. For the rest of Amsterdam, or a route through the country, open the trip planner for the Netherlands.

Cover photo: C messier, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Should I visit the Rijksmuseum or the Van Gogh Museum?
faqs.a: Choose the Rijksmuseum for breadth: Rembrandt, Vermeer and eight centuries of Dutch art and history, in three hours or more. Choose the Van Gogh Museum to follow one painter from his first works to his last in under two hours.

faqs.q: Can you do the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. They are a few minutes apart on Museumplein. Book the two time slots at least three hours apart and take the larger Rijksmuseum first.

faqs.q: How long does the Van Gogh Museum take?
faqs.a: An hour and a half to two hours for the permanent collection. The Rijksmuseum needs two hours for the famous rooms and three to four for a comfortable visit.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum in advance?
faqs.a: Yes. Both admit visitors by start time, reserved online, and the Van Gogh Museum in particular sells out days ahead in the busy months. Visitors under eighteen enter free but still need a timed ticket.

faqs.q: Is The Starry Night in the Van Gogh Museum?
faqs.a: No. The Starry Night is in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The Amsterdam museum has the Potato Eaters, the Sunflowers, the Bedroom, Almond Blossom and Wheatfield with Crows.

title: Brussels on foot, from the Grand-Place to the upper town: what is free and what needs a ticket
subtitle: One slope, forty minutes of walking, half a day with the stops. Most of it costs nothing.
excerpt: A walk through the centre of Brussels, from the Grand-Place and Manneken-Pis up past the cathedral and the Mont des Arts to the royal quarter and the Sablon: what you see for free, which doors need a ticket, and what the partner sells along the way.
longtail_phrases: is the Grand-Place in Brussels free
how long does it take to walk around central Brussels
is the Manneken-Pis the original statue
which museums in Brussels need a ticket
where is the best free view of Brussels
meta_title: Brussels on foot: Grand-Place to the upper town
meta_description: A walk from the Grand-Place and Manneken-Pis up to the Mont des Arts, the royal quarter and the Sablon: what is free and which doors need a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The Gothic Town Hall of Brussels with its tall spire and a row of guild houses on the Grand-Place

content_html:
[place attraction="grand-place" city="brussels"]

On the evening of 13 August 1695 a French army under Marshal de Villeroy, drawn up on the high ground west of Brussels, began to fire mortar bombs and red-hot shot into the city. Louis XIV wanted to draw his enemies away from the siege of Namur. The firing went on until the 15th. The gunners took the spire of the Town Hall as their mark, and when the fires died down some four thousand houses were gone, those around the main square among them. The spire was still standing.

The guilds rebuilt their houses on the square within about five years, in stone, to designs the city had to approve. That is why the Grand-Place looks as if it had been made in one piece. It is also the start of the best short walk in Brussels: from the merchants' town at the bottom of the slope to the royal quarter at the top, forty minutes without stops and half a day with them. Most of it costs nothing.

Lower town, upper town

Brussels grew on a hillside. Trade and the guilds were at the bottom, beside a river that now runs underground. The court was at the top, on the hill called Coudenberg. Central Station sits between the two, five minutes from the Grand-Place.

The walk below goes uphill, because most visitors begin at the square. If your legs prefer it, take a tram or the metro to the top and do it in reverse.

Around the Grand-Place

The square

The square itself is free at any hour, and is at its best early in the morning and after dark, when the fronts are lit. The Town Hall, of the fifteenth century, carries a spire about 96 metres high with a gilded St Michael on top. Facing it is the Maison du Roi, which never housed a king: it was rebuilt in Gothic style in the 1870s and holds the Brussels City Museum, which needs a ticket. The inside of the Town Hall is seen on guided visits, also with a ticket.

Manneken-Pis

Five minutes to the south-west, on a street corner, is a bronze boy about 55 centimetres tall. The figure in the niche is a copy placed there in 1965. The original, cast in 1619 by Jérôme Duquesnoy, is in the City Museum. He is often dressed: his wardrobe has passed a thousand costumes. Looking is free.

Manneken-Pis in his niche. The statue on the corner is a copy. Photo: Benoit Brummer (Trougnouf), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The arcades and the Bourse

North-east of the square, the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert opened in 1847, among the first glass-roofed shopping arcades in Europe. Walking through costs nothing. West of the square stands the Bourse, the former stock exchange of 1873, whose great hall is now a public passage. The beer museum on its upper floors, Belgian Beer World, needs a ticket.

The Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert, opened in 1847, in the evening. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The climb: cathedral and Mont des Arts

Behind Central Station, the Cathedral of St Michael and St Gudula was begun in 1226 and took nearly three centuries to finish. Its nave is free to enter.

From the station, steps lead up through the Mont des Arts, a formal garden laid out in the 1950s. Turn round at the top: this is the free view of Brussels, with the spire of the Town Hall rising out of the lower town.

From the top of the Mont des Arts: the garden, the lower town and the spire of the Town Hall. Photo: iMahesh, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A few steps higher is the Old England building, a department store of 1899 in iron and glass. It houses the Musical Instruments Museum, which needs a ticket.

The upper town

Place Royale is a white, symmetrical square of the 1770s, built over the ruins of the old palace of the dukes of Brabant, which burned down in 1731. What survives of that palace lies under the paving and can be visited, with a ticket, as the Coudenberg. The Royal Museums of Fine Arts and the Magritte Museum are on the same square, each with its ticket.

A minute away, the Royal Palace faces the park. It is the king's place of work, and by tradition its state rooms open to visitors without charge for some weeks in summer: check before counting on it. The BELvue Museum next door tells the history of Belgium and needs a ticket. The park is free.

From Place Royale, a straight street runs south to the Sablon. The church of Notre-Dame du Sablon is free. So is the garden opposite, the Petit Sablon, whose railings carry 48 small bronze figures, one for each of the old trades of the city. The walk ends five minutes further on, at the terrace in front of the Palace of Justice, with the widest view over the lower town. A free public lift goes down from there to the Marolles quarter.

The garden of the Petit Sablon, with the monument to the counts of Egmont and Hoorn. Photo: iMahesh, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket, in short

  • The Brussels City Museum and the guided visit of the Town Hall.
  • Belgian Beer World, in the Bourse.
  • The Musical Instruments Museum.
  • The Coudenberg, the Royal Museums of Fine Arts, the Magritte Museum and the BELvue Museum.

Everything else on the route is free. One or two interiors are enough for a day. Many museums in Brussels close on Mondays.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Central Brussels audio tour is commentary in the partner's app, in fourteen stops. It runs from Place Royale down to Manneken-Pis, the downhill direction. It includes no tickets.
  • The Musical Instruments Museum ticket with a city audio tour is entry for a time you choose and an audio walk from the museum down to the Bourse.
  • The Belgian Beer World ticket is entry, a beer on the rooftop and an audio walk through the lower town.
  • The BELvue Museum ticket with a city audio tour is entry and an audio walk through the centre.

In all three bundles the partner's audio is for the streets. It does not guide you through the rooms of the museum. Other listings in Brussels, such as the Atomium, are far from the centre and not part of this walk.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells along this route, with today's prices:

[partner city="brussels" match="central,beer,instruments,belvue" limit="4"]

From here

Below the Palace of Justice, the Marolles quarter holds a flea market every morning on Place du Jeu de Balle. The Atomium is at the northern edge of the city, reached by metro. For the rest of Brussels, or a route on to Bruges and Ghent, open the trip planner for Belgium.

Cover photo: iMahesh, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Grand-Place in Brussels free?
faqs.a: Yes. The square is a public space, open at all hours. Only the Brussels City Museum in the Maison du Roi and the guided visit of the Town Hall need a ticket.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk around central Brussels?
faqs.a: From the Grand-Place up to the Palace of Justice is about forty minutes of walking. With stops at Manneken-Pis, the arcades, the cathedral, the Mont des Arts and the Sablon, allow half a day, and longer if you enter a museum.

faqs.q: Is the Manneken-Pis on the street the original?
faqs.a: No. The statue in the niche is a copy placed there in 1965. The original of 1619 is kept in the Brussels City Museum on the Grand-Place.

faqs.q: Where is the best free view of Brussels?
faqs.a: From the top of the steps of the Mont des Arts, looking over the garden to the spire of the Town Hall, and from the terrace in front of the Palace of Justice.

faqs.q: Which sights in central Brussels need a ticket?
faqs.a: The City Museum, the Town Hall visit, Belgian Beer World, the Musical Instruments Museum, the Coudenberg, the Royal Museums of Fine Arts, the Magritte Museum and the BELvue Museum. The squares, churches, arcades, gardens and viewpoints are free.

title: Gamla Stan on foot: a two-hour route through Stockholm's old town, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: An island you can cross in fifteen minutes, six stops worth making, and five doors that charge.
excerpt: A two-hour walking route through Gamla Stan, the old town of Stockholm, from the Royal Palace to Riddarholmen: what is free, which buildings need a ticket, when to go, and what the partner's audio walks include.
secondary_keywords: what to see in Gamla Stan
longtail_phrases: how long do you need in Gamla Stan
is Gamla Stan free to visit
what time is the changing of the guard in Stockholm
where is the narrowest street in Stockholm
do you need a ticket for the Royal Palace in Stockholm
meta_title: Gamla Stan on foot: a two-hour route, and what is free
meta_description: A two-hour route through Stockholm's old town, from the Royal Palace to Riddarholmen: what is free, which five doors need a ticket, and when to go.

featured_image.alt: The coloured gabled houses of Stortorget, the main square of the old town of Stockholm, with benches and a stone well

content_html:
[place attraction="stortorget" city="stockholm"]

In the first days of November 1520, Christian II of Denmark was crowned king of Sweden in Stockholm and gave three days of feasts in the castle. On the evening of the 7th the gates were shut. His guests, Swedish nobles, bishops and townsmen who had fought him and had been promised a pardon, were accused of heresy. Over the next two days more than eighty of them were beheaded or hanged in the main square, Stortorget.

One of the dead was the father of a young nobleman, Gustav Eriksson, who raised a rebellion, drove the Danes out and was elected king on 6 June 1523. Sweden still keeps that date as its national day. The square where it began is now the quiet centre of Gamla Stan, an island you can cross in fifteen minutes. Walking it is free. The buildings along the way are not, and it helps to know which are worth entering.

How the old town is laid out

Gamla Stan is one main island with a small one, Riddarholmen, joined to its western side by a bridge. Stockholm was founded here in the middle of the thirteenth century, at the point where Lake Mälaren runs out into the Baltic. The palace and the cathedral stand at the northern end, Stortorget is in the middle, and one long shopping street, Västerlånggatan, runs the length of the island.

The metro station Gamla stan is on the western shore. From Central Station it is ten minutes on foot, over the bridges beside the parliament. The lanes are cobbled and several are steep.

A two-hour route

1. The palace courtyard

The Royal Palace replaced a castle that burned down in 1697. It was finished in 1754, has more than six hundred rooms, and is still where the king works. The changing of the guard in the outer courtyard, around midday, is free, and in summer it often comes with a military band. The time varies with the season.

A military band at the changing of the guard, in the outer courtyard of the palace. Photo: W. Bulach, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

2. Storkyrkan and the smallest statue

The brick cathedral beside the palace was consecrated in 1306. Inside is a wooden St George and the Dragon of 1489, carved to celebrate a victory over the Danes in 1471. The cathedral charges visitors for entry. In the yard behind the Finnish Church, a few steps away, sits the Iron Boy, a figure about fifteen centimetres high that people dress in knitted hats in winter.

3. Stortorget

The square of the opening story: tall merchants' houses in red, yellow and green, and a stone well. The long building on its north side, the old Stock Exchange of the 1770s, is the seat of the Swedish Academy and holds the Nobel Prize Museum.

4. Köpmantorget

Two minutes east, a bronze copy of St George and the Dragon stands in the open air. If you did not pay to enter the cathedral, this is your look at it.

The bronze copy of St George and the Dragon on Köpmantorget. The wooden original is inside the cathedral. Photo: Arild Vågen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

5. Prästgatan and the narrowest alley

Prästgatan runs parallel to Västerlånggatan and is nearly empty. At its corner with Kåkbrinken a Viking-age runestone is built into the foot of a wall. Follow the lane south to Mårten Trotzigs gränd, a stairway of 36 steps between two houses, 90 centimetres wide at its narrowest.

Prästgatan, one street away from the crowds of Västerlånggatan. Photo: Arild Vågen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Riddarholmen

Cross the bridge to the small island. Riddarholmen Church, with its openwork iron spire, is where the kings of Sweden were buried for centuries. Walk past it to the terrace on the western shore: the view runs across the water to the City Hall, where the Nobel banquet is held. It is free, and best in the evening.

Riddarholmen at dusk, seen across the water. Photo: Arild Vågen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

  • The Royal Palace. One ticket covers the state apartments, the Treasury with the crown jewels, and the museum of the old castle in the cellars. Rooms close without much notice for state occasions.
  • The Royal Armoury, in the vaults of the palace, is a separate museum with its own ticket: royal coaches, armour and costumes.
  • Storkyrkan charges an entrance fee.
  • The Nobel Prize Museum on Stortorget needs a ticket.
  • Riddarholmen Church needs a ticket and is open mainly in the warmer months.

If you have time for one interior, the palace gives the most: allow an hour and a half. Current hours are on our pages for the Royal Palace, Storkyrkan and the Nobel Prize Museum.

Reading the partner's listings

For Gamla Stan our partner sells audio walks: commentary in its app, on your own phone, with a map that leads you from stop to stop. No guide meets you, and no entry ticket is part of any of them. Tickets for the palace, the cathedral or the museums are bought separately.

The walks differ in where they start and how long they last:

  • one begins at the Gamla stan metro station and takes about two hours;
  • two begin at the palace end and finish at Riddarholmen Church after about two and a half hours;
  • one ends on the terrace of Riddarholmen, and one starts on Riddarholmen and finishes at the cathedral.

Several have almost the same name. Open each one and compare the starting point and the length with your day. Bring earphones, and download the tour before you set out.

These are the audio walks of Gamla Stan our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="stockholm" match="gamla,old town" limit="5"]

When to go

In the middle of a summer day Västerlånggatan is packed from end to end. Before ten in the morning and after six in the evening the same lanes are almost empty, and in June it stays light until late. In winter it is dark by mid-afternoon. A Christmas market fills Stortorget in December.

From here

The warship Vasa, which sank in the harbour on her first voyage in 1628 and was raised in 1961, is in the Vasa Museum on the island of Djurgården, reached by tram or by ferry. Our partner sells nothing for it, so book that one directly. South of the old town, the heights of Södermalm give the view back over its roofs. For the rest of Stockholm, open the trip planner for Sweden.

Cover photo: Øyvind Holmstad, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Gamla Stan?
faqs.a: Two hours cover the main streets and squares on foot, from the palace to Riddarholmen. Add an hour and a half if you visit the Royal Palace, and about an hour for the Nobel Prize Museum.

faqs.q: Is Gamla Stan free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. The streets, the squares, the changing of the guard and the viewpoint on Riddarholmen are free. The Royal Palace, the Royal Armoury, Storkyrkan, the Nobel Prize Museum and Riddarholmen Church charge for entry.

faqs.q: What time is the changing of the guard in Stockholm?
faqs.a: It takes place in the outer courtyard of the Royal Palace around midday, a little later on Sundays, and less often in winter. The time varies with the season, so check before you go.

faqs.q: Where is the narrowest street in Stockholm?
faqs.a: Mårten Trotzigs gränd, in the southern part of Gamla Stan: a stairway of 36 steps that narrows to 90 centimetres.

faqs.q: Do the audio walks of Gamla Stan include entry tickets?
faqs.a: No. They are commentary on your own phone, with a map of the route. Tickets for the palace, the cathedral and the museums are bought separately.

title: Copenhagen harbour on foot: from Nyhavn to Amalienborg and the Little Mermaid, and what is free
subtitle: Two and a half kilometres along the water, timed for the guard at noon. Nearly all of it costs nothing.
excerpt: A walk along the harbour of Copenhagen from Nyhavn past Amalienborg, the Marble Church, the Gefion Fountain and Kastellet to the Little Mermaid: how long it takes, when to start, what is free, and what the partner sells for it.
focus_keyword: walk from Nyhavn to the Little Mermaid
secondary_keywords: Amalienborg changing of the guard time
longtail_phrases: how far is the Little Mermaid from Nyhavn
is the Little Mermaid in Copenhagen worth seeing

meta_title: Copenhagen harbour walk: Nyhavn to the Little Mermaid
meta_description: From Nyhavn past Amalienborg, the Marble Church and Kastellet to the Little Mermaid: how long the walk takes, when to start, and what is free.

featured_image.alt: The coloured houses of Nyhavn in Copenhagen with wooden sailing boats moored along the quay

content_html:
[place attraction="amalienborg" city="copenhagen"]

In 1909 the brewer Carl Jacobsen, heir to Carlsberg, saw the ballet of The Little Mermaid at the Royal Theatre in Copenhagen and decided the city should have a statue of her. He gave the commission to the sculptor Edvard Eriksen and asked the principal dancer, Ellen Price, to model for it. She agreed to sit for the head only, so the body is that of the sculptor's wife, Eline. The bronze was set on a boulder at the edge of the harbour on 23 August 1913.

She is 1.25 metres tall. She lost her head in 1964 and again in 1998, an arm in 1984, and in 2003 she was blown off her rock altogether. Each time she was repaired. Visitors who take a coach straight to her are often let down by a small figure and a large crowd. Reached at the end of a walk along the water, she is the right size. This is that walk: about two and a half kilometres, all of it free unless you choose to go indoors.

The route at a glance

Start at Kongens Nytorv, the square with the metro station at the head of Nyhavn, and finish at the statue. Without stops the walk takes forty minutes. With them, allow two to two and a half hours.

The one thing with a fixed time is the changing of the guard at Amalienborg, at noon. To be there for it, leave Nyhavn at about eleven.

Nyhavn

The canal was dug in the 1670s, on the orders of Christian V, to bring ships from the harbour to the square. For two centuries it was a quarter of sailors and taverns. The north side takes the sun and has the coloured houses of the photographs. The oldest, number 9, dates from 1681. Hans Christian Andersen lived in three different houses on the canal, at numbers 20, 67 and 18.

Walking the quay is free. The canal boats that leave from the head of Nyhavn need a ticket, and our partner does not sell them.

Amalienborg and the Marble Church

Follow the harbour north, past the Royal Playhouse and through the small garden of Amaliehaven, and enter the palace square from the water side. Four almost identical palaces stand around an octagon. They were built in the 1750s for four noble families, and the royal family moved in after its own palace, Christiansborg, burned in 1794. The horseman in the middle is Frederik V.

Amalienborg from the harbour side: the statue of Frederik V and, on the same line, the dome of the Marble Church. Photo: Richard Mortel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Royal Life Guards, in bearskin caps, leave their barracks beside Rosenborg Castle at half past eleven, march through the city and arrive in the square at noon. Watching is free. One of the four palaces holds the Amalienborg Museum, which needs a ticket.

Inland, on the axis of the square, is Frederik's Church, called the Marble Church. It was begun in 1749, left as a roofless ruin for more than a century, and finished in 1894 with the money of a financier, C.F. Tietgen. The church is free. The dome is climbed at set times, for a fee. Across the water, on the same line, is the Opera House, opened in 2005.

The Gefion Fountain and Kastellet

Go on north along Amaliegade to the Gefion Fountain of 1908. It shows a Norse goddess driving four oxen, her own sons, who ploughed the island of Zealand out of Sweden. Beside it stands St Alban's, the English church, built of flint.

The oxen of the Gefion Fountain: the goddess's four sons, ploughing Zealand out of Sweden. Photo: mandoft, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Behind the fountain is Kastellet, a star-shaped citadel of the 1660s, ringed by a moat. It still belongs to the army, and its gates are open to walkers during the day, without charge. Inside are long red barrack rows, a church and, up on the rampart, a windmill. The path along the top of the ramparts is the best part.

One of the red barrack rows of Kastellet, which the army still uses. Photo: Moahim, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Little Mermaid

From the northern side of Kastellet it is a few minutes along the quay of Langelinie to the statue. She sits a few metres from the shore, with her back to the water. Coaches arrive from mid-morning to mid-afternoon. Early or late in the day you may have her almost to yourself. The rocks around her are slippery.

Getting back

  • Østerport station, with metro and suburban trains, is ten minutes on foot from the citadel.
  • The yellow harbour buses are boats, and part of public transport. They stop at Nordre Toldbod, near the Gefion Fountain, and run back to Nyhavn and further south on an ordinary ticket.

What is free, and what is not

  • Free: Nyhavn, the palace square and the changing of the guard, the Marble Church, the fountain, Kastellet and the statue.
  • With a ticket: the Amalienborg Museum, the climb to the dome of the Marble Church, the canal boats, and the design museum on Bredgade, a street behind the palace.

Current hours are on our pages for Amalienborg and Frederik's Church.

Reading the partner's listings

For this part of Copenhagen our partner sells audio walks: commentary in its app, on your own phone, with a map from stop to stop. No guide meets you. None includes entry to a palace or a museum, or a boat.

  • One starts at the Little Mermaid and ends at Christiansborg, about two and a half hours. It is this walk in reverse, carried on to the island of the parliament.
  • One runs from Tivoli to Kastellet in about three and a half hours, across the whole centre.
  • One of two hours ends at Amalienborg and takes in the harbour sights on the way.
  • One starts at Nyboder, the rows of yellow houses built for the navy, passes the Marble Church and Amalienborg, and ends at the Round Tower.
  • The longest, about four hours, covers most of the city.

The names are close to each other, so compare starting points and lengths. Bring earphones, and download the tour before you leave.

These are the audio walks of the harbour and the royal quarter our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="copenhagen" match="harbor,royal" limit="5"]

From here

Rosenborg Castle, where the crown jewels are kept, is a quarter of an hour inland from the Marble Church. Tivoli Gardens is at the other end of the centre, beside the main station. For the rest of Copenhagen, open the trip planner for Denmark.

Cover photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How far is the Little Mermaid from Nyhavn?
faqs.a: About two and a half kilometres along the harbour, or forty minutes on foot without stops. With Amalienborg, the Marble Church and Kastellet on the way, allow two hours or a little more.

faqs.q: Is the Little Mermaid in Copenhagen worth seeing?
faqs.a: As the end of the harbour walk, yes. The statue is only 1.25 metres tall and crowded in the middle of the day, so visitors who come by coach for her alone are often disappointed. Go early or late.

faqs.q: What time is the changing of the guard at Amalienborg?
faqs.a: At noon. The Royal Life Guards leave their barracks beside Rosenborg Castle at half past eleven and march through the city to the palace square. Watching is free.

faqs.q: Is Kastellet in Copenhagen free?
faqs.a: Yes. The citadel still belongs to the army, and its gates are open to walkers during the day without charge.

faqs.q: How do you get back from the Little Mermaid to the centre?
faqs.a: Walk ten minutes to Østerport station for the metro or a suburban train, or take a yellow harbour bus, a public boat, from Nordre Toldbod back to Nyhavn.

title: Suomenlinna from Helsinki: which ferry to take, what is free on the island, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: A sea fortress fifteen minutes from the Market Square, with no gate and no entrance fee.
excerpt: How to reach the sea fortress of Suomenlinna from Helsinki, which ferry takes a city ticket, the free route across the islands to the King's Gate, which museums charge, how long to allow, and what the partner sells.

is there an entrance fee for Suomenlinna
how long do you need on Suomenlinna
which ferry goes to Suomenlinna
is Suomenlinna worth visiting in winter

meta_description: Which ferry to take to Suomenlinna, the free walk across the fortress to the King's Gate, which museums need a ticket, and how long to allow.

featured_image.alt: The islands of Suomenlinna seen from the water, with the white tower of the fortress church above the trees

content_html:
[place attraction="suomenlinna" city="helsinki"]

In 1748 Sweden began to build a fortress on a cluster of rocky islands off Helsinki, to hold the eastern half of its kingdom against Russia. The work was led by an officer named Augustin Ehrensvärd, lasted decades and occupied thousands of soldiers. The result was one of the largest sea fortresses in Europe. The Swedes called it Sveaborg, and others called it the Gibraltar of the North.

It fell almost without a fight. In the spring of 1808 a Russian force smaller than the garrison surrounded it across the ice, and on 3 May its commander, Carl Olof Cronstedt, surrendered. Finland passed from Sweden to Russia the following year. The fortress served the tsars for 110 years, was shelled by a British and French fleet in 1855, and in 1918 was renamed Suomenlinna, the Castle of Finland. Today about eight hundred people live on it, it is a World Heritage Site, and reaching it costs a public transport ticket. What to pay for beyond that is the question.

Which ferry

The public ferry leaves from the eastern end of the Market Square, opposite the Presidential Palace. It belongs to the city's transport network, runs all year, and crosses in fifteen to twenty minutes. In the daytime there are several boats an hour, and they go on late into the evening.

The public ferry Suomenlinna II in the harbour, with ice on the water. Photo: Sinikka Halme, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

  • The ticket is an ordinary city ticket for the central zones, the same one that works on trams. A day ticket covers the crossing both ways.
  • Buy it before you board, from the machine on the quay or in the transport app. It is not sold on the boat.
  • In summer a private water bus also sails from the Market Square. It has its own tickets, the city ticket is not valid on it, and it calls at a second pier nearer the southern end of the fortress.

What is free

The fortress itself. There is no gate and no entrance fee, and because people live here, the islands are open at all hours. A signposted route, marked in blue, runs from the main quay to the King's Gate at the southern tip, about a kilometre and a half each way. Along it:

  • The Jetty Barracks. The long pink building you land beneath, from the Russian years.
  • The church. Built in 1854 as an Orthodox church for the Russian garrison and made Lutheran after independence. Its tower is also a working lighthouse.
  • The Great Courtyard. The old centre of the fortress, with the tomb of Ehrensvärd in the middle.
  • The dry dock. Begun in the 1750s, among the oldest in Europe still in use. You look down into it from the path.
  • Kustaanmiekka. The southernmost island: grassed ramparts, sandbanks, and heavy Russian guns of the nineteenth century pointing out to sea.
  • The King's Gate. The ceremonial entrance of the 1750s, on the spot where the ship of King Adolf Frederick anchored in 1752. It is the emblem of the fortress.

The dry dock, begun in the 1750s and still used for repairing wooden ships. Photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

One of the Russian coastal guns on the ramparts of Kustaanmiekka. Photo: Leonhard Lenz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The King's Gate, in the walls of Kustaanmiekka at the southern end of the fortress. Photo: Karel Frydrýšek (Fry72), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

  • The Suomenlinna Museum. In the visitor centre in the middle of the islands: the history of the fortress and a short film, shown in several languages. It is the main museum, and it stays open for most of the year.
  • The submarine Vesikko. A Finnish submarine of the 1930s, hauled up on the shore. Open in summer.
  • The smaller museums: the house of Ehrensvärd, the military museum and a toy museum, open mainly in the summer season.
  • Guided walks from the visitor centre are charged.

If you want the story before the stones, start with the museum and its film, then walk south. Current hours are on our page for the Suomenlinna Museum.

How long, and when

Allow three to four hours with the crossings: half a day. On fine summer afternoons the islands fill with people from Helsinki carrying picnics, and the boats back at about five have a queue.

In winter the ferry breaks its way through the ice, the islands are quiet and windy, most of the small museums are shut, and the paths can be icy.

  • The lanes are cobbled, and the ramparts and the cliffs have no railings. Keep small children by the hand.
  • The tunnels in the walls are unlit. Use the light of your phone.
  • It is cooler and windier than the city. Bring one more layer than you think you need.
  • There are cafés, a restaurant with its own brewery by the quay, and a small grocery shop.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Suomenlinna Museum entry ticket is admission to the museum and its film. It is not the ferry, and the fortress itself needs no ticket.
  • The SkyWheel ticket is a ride of ten to twelve minutes on the observation wheel on the quay beside the Market Square, with a view over the harbour towards the islands.
  • The audio walks are commentary in the partner's app for the centre of Helsinki. They start at Senate Square or the cathedral and pass the Market Square, where the ferry leaves. They cover the mainland, not the islands, and include no entry. Bring earphones.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells for Suomenlinna and the harbour of Helsinki, with today's prices:

[partner city="helsinki" match="suomenlinna,harbor" limit="5"]

From here

Back on the Market Square, the stalls sell berries, fish and coffee in the open air. Uspenski Cathedral, in red brick on its rock, is five minutes to the east. Senate Square and Helsinki Cathedral are two blocks inland. For more on the fortress and the rest of Helsinki, or a longer route, open the trip planner for Finland.

Cover photo: Pudelek (Marcin Szala), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Suomenlinna from Helsinki?
faqs.a: By the public ferry from the eastern end of the Market Square. It runs all year, takes fifteen to twenty minutes, and uses an ordinary city transport ticket bought before boarding.

faqs.q: Is there an entrance fee for Suomenlinna?
faqs.a: No. The fortress has no gate and no entrance fee, and the islands are open at all hours. You pay for the ferry and for any museum you choose to enter.

faqs.q: How long do you need on Suomenlinna?
faqs.a: Three to four hours including the crossings. That covers the walk from the main quay to the King's Gate and back, with time for the Suomenlinna Museum.

faqs.q: Which museums on Suomenlinna need a ticket?
faqs.a: The Suomenlinna Museum, which stays open for most of the year, and in summer the submarine Vesikko, the Ehrensvärd Museum, the military museum and the toy museum.

faqs.q: Is Suomenlinna worth visiting in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, if you dress for wind and ice. The ferry runs through the winter and the islands are quiet, but most of the small museums are closed and the paths can be slippery.
